excerpt: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brough
body: Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week
The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period
In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas
A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people
Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region
More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas
At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes
On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing

title: How the Government Wastes Our Time
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Americans are bogged down in paperwork for reasons that are sometimes necessary, so
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Americans are bogged down in paperwork for reasons that are sometimes necessary, sometimes thoughtless—and, at times, nefarious

In her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It , my colleague Annie Lowrey looks at all those hours spent looking for tax documents or trying to certify income for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, or the FAFSA and finds that things don’t have to be this way
A time tax is an infliction of “paperwork, effort, delay, and aggravation” that Americans suffer to get the rights they are guaranteed

We have the right to vote in a democracy; a time tax creates obstacles to those rights and makes realizing them cumbersome: They show up as extra identification requirements, when voter fraud is incredibly rare—or, in Jim Crow, as literacy tests
If I get hungry, I can order food from just about anywhere with just a few swipes of my thumb; one click at midnight, and diapers can be at the door before the sun rises

Why is there still such sludge in our bureaucratic systems? On this episode of Radio Atlantic , Annie joins me to discuss how these time taxes show up in our lives and waste our time, and how to make our government more efficient

The following is a transcript of the episode: Annie Lowrey: I think if instead of saying, This is about the poor people getting this program , or This is about making sure that these programs are secure , we could have a politics that says, This is malign; this is bad policy making
We give the government $8 trillion a year, and it passes back this garbage? No! No. [ Music ] Adam Harris: This is Radio Atlantic
I’m Adam Harris, and today we need to think about all of the ways that the government wastes our time

If you’ve ever thought to yourself while filling out your taxes or trying to cancel a gym membership that This is taking too long! Don’t they already have this information? There has to be a better way! —you’re not alone

My colleague Annie Lowrey has a name for these cumbersome processes: She calls them “time taxes.” She wrote about the phenomenon for The Atlantic in 2021, and in her new book, The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time—And How to Fix It , she explores how and why our time is squandered when it does not have to be
So, what gets lost in the hours spent filling out paperwork? And how do we fix it? Annie joins me now to discuss
Annie Lowrey: Thank you for having me, Adam
Harris: So, I wanna start by talking about the DMV

Harris: Because, right, it’s Labor Day, government offices are closed, but tomorrow across the country, DMVs are gonna be full of people trying to renew their car registrations, get Real IDs, change their addresses, change their names—whatever it might be

But those long lines at the DMV, I think, are the most trenchant example of what you call a “time tax.” So what are time taxes, and how do they show up in everyday lives, even outside of the DMV? Lowrey: So time taxes, these show up everywhere you are encountering the government, and really everywhere you’re interacting with businesses, right? It doesn’t necessarily have to be the government
And a time tax—or what’s called in the academic literature “an administrative burden”—is merely the person who is being bureaucratized, their experience of bureaucracy

So how much work they have to do to apply to something; how much work they have to do to research it; the fees that they might have to pay in some cases; and also their psychological or emotional experience, whether that’s DMV-level frustration or emotional anguish in a welfare program, or even a sense of civic pride that you might get when you’re interacting with a service that makes you feel good about yourself
Harris: So this is how people sort of interact with different things, right? So like you said, it’s not just the government—it can also be canceling a gym membership
In your new book, The Time Tax , you write about the idea that we see some of the most cumbersome examples of these time taxes as they relate to sort of social-safety-net programs
Food stamps, Medicaid, Social Security—things that people in need of help need to survive

So why is that? Why do we see a structure where the time taxes seem so cumbersome in those social-safety-net programs? Lowrey: We see time taxes as a general point, I think, being bigger, more onerous, more expensive in a broad sense of the word for programs that are affecting people with less social status, for whatever reason that might be—people with a history of being discriminated against, people viewed with some kind of skepticism by the state
So that could be people who weren’t born here, immigrants
That could be people with a history of interaction or involvement with the criminal-justice system
White Americans are treated very differently than Black Americans
And absolutely, high-income Americans are treated very different than low-income Americans
And importantly, I don’t think that’s because low-income Americans are the recipients of this generosity that high-income Americans aren’t
So high-income Americans, they absolutely use programs like Social Security retirement benefits
They use tax programs like the 529 college-savings program or the Home Mortgage Interest Deduction
They benefit from the exclusion of employer-sponsored health benefits in some cases
But we don’t think of those as benefits, right? Those are tax policies—that’s not a benefit
To the government, in accounting terms, it’s the same thing

It’s just that we’re not asking you to pee in a cup for it, which we do for a lot of benefits where you have to apply and reapply and come face-to-face with a social worker and perhaps fill out forms that might be a hundred pages long
And none of those policies interact with each other; they’re really cumbersome
And I think that’s because we want to dissuade low-income people from using these, because we believe that some share of them are applying fraudulently
And there’s this thought that, you know, Maybe if you’re low income, you need to get a little bit better at paperwork in your life
You need to straighten up and figure yourself out
And this is an imposition of that moral onto you
Harris: Yeah, and it’s interesting that you mentioned all the paperwork, and that’s even if they know that the programs exist to help them, right? Lowrey: Absolutely
Harris: And that doesn’t—as you write, that’s not by accident, that historically these sort of cumbersome processes have been used as a form of social control that is as old as data itself

title: The Last Thing Teenagers Will Let You Teach Them
excerpt: A strange thing happened to me in a deserted parking lot on a recent Sunday morning: My 16-year-old daughter actually asked me a question
body: A strange thing happened to me in a deserted parking lot on a recent Sunday morning: My 16-year-old daughter actually asked me a question

I was telling her everything I know about reversing a car without the help of a backup camera. “First turn your whole body, shoulders rotated, right hand on the back of the passenger seat, until you’re looking out the rear window at the world behind you.” Her hands were on the wheel
Her phone was face down in the cup holder

She turned her body the way I’d suggested and nudged the wheel to the left, and the car floated backward in a woozy arc that wasn’t quite what she’d intended. “Wait,” she said. “Do I turn with both hands? Did I do that wrong?” I want to stop here, because I don’t think I can convey just how unusual such an exchange is these days—her listening to me and asking for help
Sometime in the past year, she stopped wanting anything from me other than my credit card and maybe my nicest suede boots
She definitely stopped wanting my instruction, my opinion, my take on anything, having concluded that she already understands pretty much everything
For 14 or 15 years, my daughter narrated in a fire hose of chatter—to me, to her father, to whoever
So much talking: about why the sun sets, the kid she was mad at, the plot of a show she was three episodes into, how she wanted to decorate her room
Around the start of high school, the talking thinned out, siphoned almost exclusively to her friends
It went the way a baby tooth goes, loose for a while and then simply absent. [ Helen Lewis: I’m the driver now ] When she got a learner’s permit, some measure of talking reappeared
It wasn’t fully restored, exactly, but confined within one small, sealed space that moves
Inside the car, she knows she doesn’t know: In no version of parallel parking can she wing it without asking for tips from someone who has done it 10,000 times
Learning to drive is something she cannot fake her way through
This wobbly uncertainty, this return to a kind of innocence, is the rarest condition in a 16-year-old, and it lasts about as long as a learner’s permit does

So my daughter asks, and listens, and we manage to simply talk in some of the ways we haven’t in a long time: about what her friends did over the summer, which kid at the pool where she lifeguards asked her if she could babysit them
For an hour at a stretch I get a version of my daughter that I had filed away as gone for good
But this is also, in some ways, the worst hour of my week, because the terms of a driving lesson are the exact inverse of the many other kinds of lessons that came before it

Everything else I ever taught my daughter, I did with one hand on the thing: I steadied the tail end of the bike, I held the knife and moved her fingers back from the blade, I grasped her hand crossing Seventh Avenue for so many years that my palm still expects to find hers at intersections
In the car, though, she has the wheel, and I have the fear
My only instrument is my voice, which is not connected to anything that stops the car
Parents say they’re letting go or loosening the reins or handing over the keys , as if adolescence were a series of small, deliberate releases, each one manageable
Then you hand over the actual keys, and the metaphor becomes a physical arrangement staged on a public road at 40 miles an hour, at which point it breaks
First there is supervised driving, and soon there is nothing
In between, the passenger seat is one of the few places on Earth where a parent gets to occupy two conditions at once: maximum proximity plus zero control
I have thought about this a lot from that seat, just 18 inches from my daughter, slowly understanding that being nearby was never the same as keeping her safe
Ever since she was born, I had assumed that being close to her was a form of protecting her
In the car, that assumption comes apart, and all I can do is sit there with my fear

What surprised me is that the fear runs both ways. [ Read: Let your kids fail ] For the first time in years, my daughter is frightened of something in front of both of us rather than scared of something I might do to embarrass her—that is, afraid of me
That distinction turns out to be enormous

Since she hit adolescence, her anxiety, in my presence, has generally been about whether I would say something wacky (yes!), make a dumb joke (also yes!), or exist too loudly in a space containing her peers (duh)
I have been the weather she is bracing against
But in the car, we are braced against the same thing, and it is outside the windshield
A massive truck backs out without looking; a cyclist suddenly appears
We both suck in air at the same instant, and her hand and my hand tighten—hers on the wheel, mine on nothing

Coming to a stop at a red light, she sees me sending a text from the passenger seat. “I can’t understand how anyone texts and drives,” she says, almost bewildered, the way a fifth grader might talk about someone doing calculus in their head

At that moment, she is using every part of her brain to keep a two-ton object between two painted lines, and the idea that a person could do this and tap out a message strikes her as physically impossible
I agree with her, but what I don’t say is that practicing will help her rethink this
One day she will be good enough at driving to consider being more careless about it
As she improves and gains confidence, the driving, for her, slowly grows less frightening and more thrilling

She presses the accelerator, her foot more sure, and we both know that she is on the edge of a huge new expanse of freedom and change—that driving lessons are not about a test to pass but a way to get farther than she has ever gotten on her own

title: The DSA’s Problem Isn’t ‘Media Training’
excerpt: American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem
body: American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem

In the past year, members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest leftist organization, have won electoral victories in places such as New York City and Michigan, drawing a spotlight that the group has struggled to handle
Last month, the DSA’s co-chairs, Megan Romer and Ashik Siddique, gave several high-profile interviews that even many of their most fervent supporters agree were disastrous
The two leaders struggled to give straight answers to simple questions, and they defended outlandish policies, such as abolishing prisons and police
They seemed to present socialists exactly the way their opponents caricature them: as extremist, unserious, and unprepared
In damage-control mode, many of DSA’s defenders on social media are repeating the phrase media training as though it were a mantra
If only the group’s leaders had been better prepared to deal with media outlets , the thinking goes, they would have avoided this train wreck
The DSA’s communications director, Priscilla Yeverino, recently told Axios , “Our leaders aren’t politicians

They’re working-class people and new to doing media.” The idea that the DSA’s troubles on prime-time television are a technical matter solvable by the right training is surely comforting, but it is also wrong

The group has a bigger problem: It is led by unpractical extremists whose views are a far cry from those that its electorally successful figures, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, espouse. [ Read: Why do rich kids love socialism? ] This disconnect is partly explained by a sharp division within the DSA
One wing engages in mass politics and includes AOC, Mamdani, and other socialists committed to democratic principles
The other wing is sectarian and extremist: It evinces little commitment to democracy and includes open admirers of Hamas, the Iranian regime, and historical dictators such as Mao Zedong
If the interviews with the DSA’s co-chairs were embarrassing, that’s a result not of a lackluster media performance but of the actual positions the group has embraced
A closer look at the interviews confirms this

Romer, who belongs to the sectarian wing, evidently did not know what the 2000 Camp David Summit was and could not say what “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” as she demanded, would look like in practice
When asked about authoritarianism in Cuba, she praised the country’s constitution and suggested that Americans should learn from it
Maybe media training could have taught Romer what happened at Camp David and what a tax policy might entail
It still wouldn’t have made the pro-authoritarian politics she shares with her faction of the DSA more palatable
In December, Romer’s Red Star caucus, a self-declared Marxist-Leninist faction of the DSA, posted quotes from a speech by Mao in “celebration” of the Chinese Communist leader’s 132nd birthday
Members of the faction study the works of Mao and the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin as part of their political education

Red Star has declared its unequivocal sympathy for Hamas and praised the “good judgement” of “our socialist siblings” in Palestine for working with the Islamist organization and “external groups like Iran, Hezbollah, and Ansarallah under a principle they call unity of the fields .” In other words, Red Star is an admirer of Iran’s notorious “Axis of Resistance.” That Romer wouldn’t critique authoritarianism in Cuba is not a lapse but an expression of her faction’s politics
Red Star’s stated policy couldn’t be any clearer about this: “To publicly critique a government or movement that stands in opposition to the American government is to do the U.S
State Department’s work for them, from Iran to Palestine.” In other words, any state or group that opposes the American government should be beyond criticism

Liberation, the DSA’s “Marxist-Leninist-Maoist caucus,” likewise declares the United States to be “not a nation” but a “prison-house of nations, with the Euro-Americans being the jailer.” Unlike Romer, Siddique belongs to the mainstream wing of the DSA, but he is bound by the group’s statements and broader culture

The sectarian wing currently dominates the DSA: The group’s convention in Chicago last year rejected a resolution opposing “all governments that engage in the repression of democratic rights.” Thus, when asked repeatedly what he thought of Fidel Castro, whom the DSA had praised in an earlier statement, Siddique awkwardly referred to “inequality in the United States” and criticized U.S. policy—deflecting the question and offering sound bites instead of engagement, much as an establishment pol might do. [ David Brooks: Democrats became great by fighting the left ] This pro-left-authoritarian orientation explains why DSA electoral observers shamefully reported no fraud when they were dispatched to monitor the electoral sham organized by Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro in 2024
Those results were so bogus that even the left-wing governments of Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay couldn’t accept them

Yet at a DSA session on the subject, a pro-Maduro organization’s assessment that Venezuela’s electoral system was “one of the very best in the world” was presented as fact, as was the false claim that Venezuela’s main opposition candidates were “fascist.” The two wings of the DSA are committed to wildly different methods
Mamdani governs New York City partly as a technocrat, and AOC has sought to influence the Democratic Party from within

One of the DSA’s sectarian factions, by contrast, recently suggested that socialist lawmakers “should do everything in their power to disrupt any Congressional business that does not benefit the working class or advance the socialist program.” They should, it went on, “creatively abuse their powers to make it difficult to conduct legislative business,” for instance by packing the galleries of Congress with hecklers
This faction seems to view elected lawmakers as “tribunes” for the socialist movement rather than as people who, you know, make laws
The sectarian wing got the DSA to drop its endorsement of AOC and refuse to support Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election

Red Star argued against endorsing AOC unless she withdrew her support for Joe Biden (then the Democratic nominee), and it refused to fundraise for the Democratic leadership or central congressional campaign

But ultimately, the DSA dropped AOC on the grounds that she was not sufficiently anti-Israel—a singular obsession of the sectarian wing. (The foreign-policy section of the DSA’s political platform discusses the details of only one country’s politics, and that’s Israel and Palestine, in which it calls for the self-determination of Palestinians without making a similar provision for Israeli Jews.) For all of the extremist wing’s influence, however, my years of research into the group suggest that the DSA’s members are mostly not members of any caucuses

The average DSA member probably has more in common with AOC than with Mao or Hamas, and the nonsectarians seem especially dominant in the group’s large urban chapters—such as in New York City, where the DSA has more than 15,000 of its approximately 120,000 members
More than 80 percent of DSA members in the Bronx and Queens voted in 2024 to endorse AOC

The sectarian wing came to control much of the organization’s leadership by manipulating internal processes, which is one reason it opposes organizational referenda and other one-member-one-vote procedures

The DSA’s mainstream wing includes thinkers who are committed to democracy, critical of authoritarianism (including that of socialist regimes, past and present), and who reject some of the signature policies of the sectarian wing, such as police abolition
These figures have been vocal in response to last month’s media fiasco

Eric Blanc, a labor historian at Rutgers, sharply criticized Romer for “falling into a trap being set by the establishment,” which seeks “to paint DSA as extreme.” Like others in his wing, Blanc advocates for adopting a Nordic-style social democracy as a step toward overcoming capitalism

This position is also shared by the Jacobin founder and former DSA Vice Chair Bhaskar Sunkara, whose 2019 Socialist Manifesto explores Swedish social democracy in envisioning a socialism for the 21st century. [ James Kirchick: The DSA is a parasite ] Reacting to the DSA’s recent media debacles, Ben Burgis, a philosopher and Jacobin writer, opined : “We don’t do ourselves any favors by refusing to say anything too negative about left-wing dictatorships targeted by US foreign policy,” especially “if we’re trying to argue that the failures of authoritarian state socialism in the twentieth century shouldn’t mean that capitalism is the best humanity will ever be able to do.” The group has failed to reassure its critics of its commitment to multiparty democracy, Burgis added

title: The Charges Were Dropped, but the Damage Was Already Done
excerpt: D avid Huerta sat on a steel bed too small for his burly frame in a Los Angeles jail last summer and looked out a small rectangular window at Dodger Stadium, wh
body: D avid Huerta sat on a steel bed too small for his burly frame in a Los Angeles jail last summer and looked out a small rectangular window at Dodger Stadium, where he’d once spent evenings with his two boys
He was the kid who’d made good, although it hadn’t been easy
His mother died from breast cancer when he was 4

He was raised in southeast L.A. by his dad, a veteran of the Korean War turned Teamster, who paid the bills by loading and unloading cargo—and, when he was out of work, took his sons with him to the hiring hall

Huerta steered clear of gangs and instead went to college, became a union organizer, and worked his way up to become president of the largest labor union in the state, the Service Employees International Union of California
He was sure that he hadn’t done anything illegal
He had screamed at masked federal agents as they executed search warrants at a downtown apparel business that was suspected of hiring undocumented immigrants
He had been angry, no question—especially at President Trump
He had flipped his middle fingers at the masked federal officers
At one point, he sat down in front of the business’s gate; later, he encouraged other protesters to form a picket circle in front of it
When an officer warned him he might be arrested, he replied, “I can’t hear you through your fucking mask.” And when a police van tried to enter, he stood with his hands on his hips nearby
He considered all of that well within the bounds of his First Amendment rights
But he couldn’t stop second-guessing his decision to show up at such a volatile scene alone
Huerta wondered how his wife and sons, his niece and nephew, and his other family members would react to seeing videos of his arrest
He wondered if he had somehow jeopardized the safety of his union’s hundreds of thousands of members by drawing unwanted headlines
He wondered if his arrest would make others more fearful of opposing this administration’s actions
He wondered when he would be released—or if he would be
He wondered if he could survive prison, should it come to that
And he wondered what his late dad would’ve thought of him sitting on a thin, stained mattress as his cellmate on the top bunk managed a comedown from drugs

Would he have been ashamed, or proud? Trump’s top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles charged Huerta with conspiracy to impede a federal officer—a felony, under a Civil War–era statute that had rarely been used before last year
If convicted, Huerta faced up to six years in prison
But months later, prosecutors lessened the charges to a misdemeanor count of obstructing, resisting, or opposing a federal officer
This July, the Justice Department said it would drop the charges altogether, adding it to the growing list of federal prosecutions that have fallen apart before going to trial
Although those dismissals have been celebrated as victories, the cases have taken a financial and psychological toll on the defendants
For Huerta, the past 15 months have been filled with anxiety
He has endured sleepless nights and grown emotionally distant from his wife of 30 years
The public attention continues to make it more difficult to do his job

And despite his pride in standing for what he believed in, he struggles with the shame of being jailed and appearing in court in shackles—an image he worries that his two sons and niece and nephew (whom he has raised as his own) will never forget

As we spoke inside a coffee shop in his neighborhood of Highland Park one recent afternoon, Huerta’s voice rose in anger and indignation while he recounted and, at times, reenacted the minutes before he was shoved to the ground by a federal officer

He teared up. “The president of the union just got fucking arrested,” he said. “If they can do this to me, imagine what they’re doing to other people.” O n the morning of June 6, 2025, the phones at the SEIU office were ringing with reported sightings of immigration-enforcement operations in and around downtown L.A
Huerta and his team—along with other labor leaders, Democrats, and social-justice groups—had been preparing for a moment like this ever since Trump was elected to a second term
The administration was trying to detain and deport as many immigrants as possible
Workplaces were being targeted, and even American-born Latinos were getting caught up in immigration dragnets
Huerta and his team would later learn that this day was the opening of a monthslong operation in the L.A. area overseen by then–Border Patrol Commander Gregory Bovino

It aimed to not just increase arrest numbers but also intimidate immigrant communities. [ Read: A U.S. citizen detained by ICE for three days tells his story ] The union’s rapid-response network was designed to help employees during moments like this. “Shit’s happening,” Huerta recalled thinking that morning, “and we’re now in the fight.” He heard a report of an immigration raid in the apparel district, so he scrapped his plans and headed there
Federal agents were swarming an industrial complex
A woman stood outside the facility’s gate, prosecutors later claimed in charging documents, filming officers and telling someone by phone what was happening
A federal agent later said that Huerta seemed to be communicating with that woman and other protesters “in a concerted effort to disrupt” the operation
As the crowd grew, people screamed expletives at the officers, and someone yelled, “I want you to kill yourself,” according to the accounts of federal agents contained in court filings

The agents described Huerta joining in the taunting, urging protesters to “walk in circles and picket,” and pacing in front of the gate, “effectively preventing law enforcement vehicles from entering or exiting.” Huerta told me that he had never acted quite like this at a protest, but that he had snapped when he saw how the officers were treating a young girl who was crying about her dad, who she said was inside the building. “They were so dismissive of her,” he said

title: The Download: the hunt for underground hydrogen and more rogue OpenAI agents

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
How much hydrogen awaits us underground? A flurry of exploration efforts is searching for underground stores of hydrogen gas, which could provide a valuable source of zero-carbon fuel

The hunt has spread all over the world and engaged dozens of startups, including the Bill Gates–backed Koloma, which has been poking around the US Midwest to reach ancient oceanic rocks associated with hydrogen production
But the search so far has come up short.  No one has yet reported finding a commercially viable reservoir of the gas, and public data on what has been found remains in short supply
Yet researchers estimate that trillions of tons of H₂ are produced within Earth’s crust
If a small fraction could be recovered, it could meet global hydrogen demand for centuries
Follow the global race to find hydrogen underground . —James Dinneen This story is from our latest print magazine, which is all about kids

One more thing What is AI? Artificial intelligence is the hottest technology of our time

But what is it? It sounds like a stupid question, but it’s one that’s never been more urgent.  Here’s the short answer: AI is a catchall term for a set of technologies that make computers do things that are thought to require intelligence when done by people

title: Your food may be safe. Its packaging is another story.
excerpt: Baby food pouches, in particular, carry a higher chemical exposure risk. | Jeffrey Greenberg, Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story was originally
body: Baby food pouches, in particular, carry a higher chemical exposure risk. | Jeffrey Greenberg, Universal Images Group via Getty Images This story was originally published by Inside Climate News and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration
Most people decide if it’s safe to eat an old tub of yogurt in the fridge or canned tuna in the back of the cupboard by checking its sell-by date
But no label indicates that pesticides, phthalates, PFAS, or other hazardous chemicals could be seeping from those containers into your food
Of more than 15,000 chemicals that come in contact with food, a new  peer-reviewed study  found that 1,222 pose serious health risks such as cancer and reproductive harm
And the vast majority — 87 percent, or more than 13,200 — lack enough accessible information to even estimate their risks

The fact that there’s not enough publicly available information for independent scientists to assess the safety of chemicals that can contaminate food is “the elephant in the room,” said study co-author Jane Muncke, managing director at the nonprofit Food Packaging Forum Foundation, which led the research, published Tuesday in the journal Environmental Science & Technology .  Consumers trust that when regulators allow chemicals in products like food packaging, it’s because it’s been through safety testing, Muncke said. “But that’s not the case,” she said. “And it doesn’t make sense.” The team has done a “very, very good job” highlighting how little is known about the risks of substances that affect everyone, said Maricel Maffini, an independent chemical safety and regulation expert who was not involved in the study but has collaborated with Muncke in the past.  Because the study focused on a list that people in industry and regulators regard as reliable, it’s looking under the proverbial lamppost, Maffini said

While there’s plenty of information suggesting that many of these chemicals should not be on the market or should have stronger regulations, she said, there’s so much information beyond that list that’s missing

In previous work, Muncke and her team identified more than 15,000 chemicals used in food processing or packaging from lists of substances approved by regulators in the United States, China, Japan, and countries in Europe and South America or that had been  identified in studies

In the new paper, they analyzed that “jaw-dropping” number of chemicals, Muncke said, to flag the most problematic.  To maximize the utility of their priority list, the team used only data obtained from governmental and regulatory agencies linking a chemical to human health hazards such as cancer, reproductive harm, or ability to concentrate in the body
That yielded a priority list of 1,222 chemicals that they ranked into four tiers, with the highest to lowest evidence of human exposure from food-contact materials

Ninety-four chemicals known to seep into food and detected in breast milk, blood, or other  human samples  were assigned to Tier 1, the highest priority for regulators and companies to consider phasing out

These chemicals include liver- and immune system-damaging PFAS “forever chemicals,” which make food wrappers grease- or water-resistant; the likely carcinogen  styrene , used to produce takeout packages and  refrigerated dairy food  containers; hormone-disrupting  phthalates , added to make plastics like those that hold  vegetable oils  flexible; and bisphenol A, added to hard plastics and can linings and a  poster child  for endocrine disruptors’ ability to impair development at low doses

Studies have found these and other chemicals leaching from containers into a diverse array of food and beverages, including  water, infant formula ,  orange juice ,  ice cream ,  yogurt and cream ,  oils, cake, and fatty foods
The next highest priority list, Tier 2, included an additional 264 hazardous chemicals that  leach into food  but have not been detected in biomonitoring studies

Recommendations to protect consumers Experts with the Food Packaging Forum say regulators can take simple steps to reduce people’s exposure to harmful chemicals found or used in food-contact materials, starting with moving away from evaluating one chemical at a time
People are exposed to multiple synthetic chemicals simultaneously through food-contact materials, textiles, personal-care products, air pollution, and more
Regulators should introduce a “mixture allocation factor,” which creates a safety margin that accounts for the combined effects of multiple chemicals in a single exposure

If there is sufficient evidence that individual chemicals in a group with similar structures and properties are hazardous, then all members of that group should be pulled from the market or not approved until proven safe, as the European Union did in its 2023 proposal to restrict PFAS as a group

Modify rules for material safety to ensure that what escapes from products is safe under different use conditions and expand screening of toxicity to include chronic disease outcomes like diabetes, infertility, and harm to the immune and nervous systems
Determine if chemicals or materials like glass or stainless steel classified as inert leach into food
If they don’t leach, they’re not a priority for in-depth chemical analysis
Inert materials that can be reused should be the policy goal
The chemicals in Tier 1 provide the most reliable evidence that materials that come in contact with food are a source of people’s exposure to these chemicals, Muncke said

The chemicals are in people, they’re in food, and they’re in food-contact materials, she said. “What more proof do you want?” Inside Climate News asked the American Chemistry Council and Food Packaging Coalition, trade groups that represent the chemical and food-packing industries, if their members would release hazard information about the chemicals they use and phase out those known to be hazardous

Neither responded, but the Food Packaging Coalition maintains that packaging is designed to prevent the transfer of its components to food and to ensure that they are safe and suitable for their intended use.  The paper offers a practical and transparent roadmap for using the best available evidence to prioritize food-contact chemicals for regulation, said Sara Lupolt, an expert on exposure assessment at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, who was not involved in the research.  Though not addressed in the paper, she added, more research is needed to determine which foods and chemical combinations result in more chemicals moving into food
Plastic chemicals in baby food Many of the chemicals that migrate into food are so-called non-intentionally added substances, (NIAS)

Their identity is often obscure because existing tools can’t identify every chemical in use, especially when researchers don’t know what to look for because producers keep proprietary chemical ingredients secret
Muncke is particularly concerned about babies’ exposure to plastic chemicals in pouches that hold juices and pureed food
Earlier this year, her team found evidence that more than 330 chemicals leach from pouches, including nearly 80 known to be hazardous
They presented the findings at  an event  at the House of Lords in the United Kingdom in June
A greater volume of chemicals gets into baby food because the ratio of packaging to food is much greater in a small serving size, Muncke said

And the pouches are sterilized using heat, which drives chemicals to migrate and forms microplastics.  Several  peer-reviewed  studies, including a  2023 Chemosphere study , also found chemicals, including NIAS, in baby food packaged in pouches

The paper’s authors believed the NIAS, which lacked adequate information to assess risk, were impurities and raw materials from producing plastic. “Infants may be constantly exposed to NIAS via consuming pouched food products,” the authors warned

For the 87 percent of chemicals that lack hazard data, it’s primarily a question of the data not being public, said study co-author Helene Wiesinger, a chemist and Food Packaging Forum scientific officer.  That delays regulatory action, Wiesinger said, because governments and independent scientists must first figure out which chemicals are safe
She believes a product or chemical should not be allowed on the market until a company can prove that it’s safe
At a minimum, chemicals that have structural similarities with others known to be hazardous should be priorities for regulation, the paper argues

Seventy percent of the more than 4,200 chemicals the team classified into 38 priority groups — including PFAS, phthalates and organophosphates (used as flame retardants and pesticides, among other applications) — lack enough data to assess potential harms
Just because something isn’t yet known to be hazardous doesn’t mean it’s not hazardous, Wiesinger said

Time and again, chemicals found to present unreasonable risks are replaced with others that have similar properties and ultimately similar risks. “We hope this work provides practical guidance on how to at least not make the very obvious mistakes,” she said.

title: Data centers are bringing Americans together
excerpt: Protesters rally against data centers at the Texas State Capitol in Austin, Texas, on July 27, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images
body: Protesters rally against data centers at the Texas State Capitol in Austin, Texas, on July 27, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images The data center backlash has entered the midterms conversation.  Politicians from across the spectrum have changed their minds — or at least their policy positions — about data centers in the past few months as public resistance to their construction has skyrocketed
A major example is Texas, where just about one year ago, Republican Gov

Greg Abbott was proclaiming that his state was the “epicenter of AI development.” Now, after months of grassroots organizing and community outcry, Abbott is pushing to slow the roll of new data centers in Texas
He’s imposed a statewide moratorium on new construction pending an audit over the new connections to Texas’s power grid
While he hasn’t explicitly said the change is tied to his reelection campaign this November, the pause is expected to last through the election
As dramatic as Abbott’s about-face has been, he’s not alone: Democrats and Republicans alike are following suit

Jeremy Merrill , a data reporter at the Washington Post, analyzed thousands of social media posts and newsletters to see what elected officials on both sides of the aisle are saying about data centers

He spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about his findings, what they say going into midterm elections, and how the backlash might change the way we think about what politicians owe to their constituents
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  What did you find? Data centers didn’t used to be a big deal
And now, almost all of a sudden, they’re a big issue
Candidates are falling over themselves to sound tough about data centers
And data centers are overwhelmingly portrayed as a problem rather than an opportunity or a benefit.  A great example is Sen
Jon Husted, who’s a Republican senator from Ohio, who’s up for election this November

He used to praise data center projects that were coming to Ohio when he was lieutenant governor because it would help establish Ohio as “an important tech hub in America.” He said that data centers are essential to our digital lives

And now he’s saying he’s trying to “protect Americans from having to foot the bill for data centers.” He’s really emblematic of a shift that happened all across the Republican Party in about February of this year

That’s when the bulk of messages from Republicans about data centers flipped from focusing on them as bringing benefits to their states and communities, to talking about their downsides.  This is really a case of the anger and unhappiness bubbling up from everyday people up to political elites

And that grassroots anger was all across the political spectrum over a whole range of issues: power bills, claims about how much water data centers may use, air pollution, eminent domain, taxes, subsidies, and a generalized, physical manifestation of the anxiety that people feel about what AI is going to do to our society, to our brains, to our kids and to our jobs

We know that it’s not just one single candidate, maybe even not just a handful, because you reported that the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that, “Data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”  That’s pretty strong language

Is the National Republican Senatorial Committee admitting that the wrong position on data centers is enough to lose a candidate a race at this point? I think it’s something that they’re certainly worried about

And presumably you’re looking for an edge, or to prevent your opponent from getting an edge over you.  What about President Donald Trump’s messaging on data centers? He, initially at least, was very bullish on AI investment in the US
What has Trump been saying? This is a story in two or three parts

As President Trump took office again last year, he was overall trying to portray his second term as president as “inaugurating a golden age for American manufacturing and technological dominance.” As part of that, he issued an executive order trying to make it easier to build data centers in the United States

And I think that’s probably why last year most Republicans across the board were talking about data centers as a benefit to the country and to the communities where they were being built — talking about jobs, talking about investment
And so on the one hand, you have President Trump promoting this bill that would protect people from having data centers cause their power bills to go up

But on the other hand, he just wrote earlier this week on Truth Social, “If [communities] want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.” He’s saying if they don’t want data centers, they’re going to “end up being backwards and poor.” So he’s still very pro-data center, which is fascinating
Which Democrats in particular are we seeing change their minds? There are a lot of governors who used to be very positive on data centers in their states because these bring jobs
These bring construction investments, some amount of permanent jobs, some amount of construction jobs
Examples of folks who are now limiting data centers in their states include Gov
Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania and [Gov.] J.B
The most striking case of a Democrat whose rhetoric has shifted so much is Rep
Ro Khanna of California, whose district actually includes Silicon Valley
In 2025, he was calling for building more data centers in the United States versus overseas

When the Trump administration did an AI deal with the United Arab Emirates, he said, “Why are we putting data centers and research hubs in Dubai?”  But now he’s more critical, calling for an end to data center extraction, taking communities’ water and jacking up their bills, sucking all the money into the hands of a few tech billionaires
Is anyone in either party still coming out strong for data centers? My favorite example of this is Rep
Eric Burlison, who’s a Republican from Missouri
He’s really focused on the need to build data centers in order to compete with China

In June, he wrote, “Ask yourself who benefits when Americans turn against data centers? China does.” He’s making the point that I think a lot of people in tech are making, which is, “This is coming whether you like it or not.” And part of politics is dealing with reality

In this day and age, it seems constituents don’t want to deal with that reality, but clearly there are people who hold office, or who hope to hold office, who are going to maintain the line that this is something we’ve just got to do
This is a classic political science dispute about what a politician’s job is supposed to be

title: This Tiny E-Reader Is the Single Best Piece of Technology in Years
excerpt: No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking
body: No matter how you read it, The Power Broker is a serious undertaking
The paperback weighs as much as a brick; to avoid lugging around all 1,344 pages, people have cut it apart at the spine and chunked it into sections
Others have organized in-person Power Broker marathon readings that run continuously for three full days
Over the past several weeks, I’ve spent 10 hours paging through Robert Caro’s masterpiece on an e-reader the size of a credit card

It’s magnetic, and small enough to attach to the back of my iPhone without adding any real bulk to my pocket. (Yes, this does mean that I have a screen on the back of another screen.) It’s called the Xteink X3, and at a glance, it looks like a cheap gimmick: more electronic junk made by unknown brands and sold on Temu and TikTok Shop—the kind of thing influencers are always hawking. (Can I interest you in a programmable LED hat for $11.60? Or how about $20 AirPod look-alikes made by “Fhumsh”?) In a sense, it is that

Xteink sounds less like a real brand name than the kind of garbled text you’ll find in AI-slop memes. (Speaking of which, the official website of the China-based company is full of AI-generated photos of people posing with the device.) And indeed, since the X3’s release on Amazon in May, TikTokers and YouTubers have raved about how the device is a steal and you should buy it right now—just click the link in bio. [ From our August 2026 issue: The end of reading is here ] And so I did
On Amazon, the X3 is $69 and tops the “hot new releases” list for e-readers, beating out a slew of Kindles
In person, the Xteink is many things: plasticky
Nevertheless, it is the single best piece of technology that I have purchased in years
In the two months before getting this cartoonishly tiny e-reader, I finished only one book
In one month with the X3, I read three books without even really trying—and my iPhone’s average daily screen time dipped by 25 minutes

The X3 is great because of its size, not in spite of it. (For once, “fun-size” actually lives up to the billing.) Because this is such a runt of a device, you can stick it to your phone and have an e-reader in your pocket at all times
As a result, I’ve found myself reading on my morning commute, in line at a museum, even while waiting through Netflix ads
The display on my Xteink may be roughly half the size of the smallest Kindle, but the text is big enough to easily read
Even after three straight hours of inching through The Power Broker , my eyes weren’t strained

The device’s size actually helped me develop a different relationship to reading altogether: Because each “page” on the Xteink amounts to just a paragraph or two—and sometimes less—I’m compelled to finish it
And now that I’m onto the next page, I might as well finish that one too

A YouTuber who recently reviewed the Xteink had the same experience—she referred to the uniquely addictive experience of using the device as the “TikTokification of reading.” I know how terrifying that sounds, but consider the outcome: Whenever there’s even a couple of minutes of free time, I now have a healthy alternative to doomscrolling on Instagram
Flip over the Bad Screen and fire up the Good Screen
For all of its charm, the Xteink is a pretty basic piece of hardware
Other popular e-readers now come with AI-powered recaps, high-definition displays, and Android operating systems

Meanwhile, the Xteink has no touch screen, color display, or backlight for reading in the dark. (Xteink recently launched the X4 Pro, a slightly larger and more expensive model that has a reading light and a touch screen.) Just reading a book on the device isn’t necessarily seamless: The preloaded software is horrific and can’t even display book covers or properly format some text
Unlike with a Kindle, you can’t port over books from Amazon with one click
In spite of itself, the Xteink X3, in all of its 3.7 inches of glory, has become a viral hit
Online, people have posted photos of their Xteink on trips to the Austrian mountains or the Aegean Sea; one anesthesiologist says he tucks it into his scrubs

People are mounting the Xteink X3 to their kitchen hood to display recipes and are making all sorts of bespoke accessories, including 3-D-printed reading lights and a case that looks like a gun ( I’m serious )
Fans have built their own open-source firmware, Crosspoint, that considerably upgrades the device
The version I downloaded displays reading stats and an array of fonts, and it lets me screenshot pages as I read
Late last month, Crosspoint added the ability to access books on Libby, the popular library ebook app
The best thing about the Xteink is not any one feature
It’s that this tiny e-reader is fun in a way so few gadgets are anymore
Despite all our advances, the consumer-electronics landscape of 2026 is predictable and banal
Our laptops, smartphones, and tablets are thinner and more powerful than ever, but that feels like a weak substitute for innovation
Next week, Apple is poised to launch one of its most hyped products in years: a folding iPhone
But even folding smartphones are old news; Samsung released its version in 2019
After shelling out hundreds or thousands of dollars for a new gadget, you might still have to pay for subscriptions and endure annoying ads
Sometimes, your purchases aren’t even really yours
Amazon recently removed the ability to download ebooks you already own and transfer them to non-Kindle devices
In other words, we need more gadgets like the Xteink: cheap, simple, and customizable
With few exceptions, these products are now coming out of China

title: My students think it’s fine to cheat with AI. Maybe they’re onto something.
excerpt: Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET:  We’re bringing you some of our best-loved  Your Mileage May Vary  columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental
body: Editor’s note, September 6, 8 am ET:  We’re bringing you some of our best-loved  Your Mileage May Vary  columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave
The one below was originally published last year
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas
It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other
I am a university teaching assistant, leading discussion sections for large humanities lecture classes
This also means I grade a lot of student writing — and, inevitably, see a lot of AI writing too.  Of course, many of us are working on developing assignments and pedagogies to make that less tempting
But as a TA, I only have limited ability to implement these policies

And in the meantime, AI-generated writing is so ubiquitous that to take course policy on it seriously, or even to escalate every suspected instance to the professor who runs the course, would be to make dozens of accusations, some of them false positives, for basically every assignment
I believe in the numinous, ineffable value of a humanities education, but I’m also not going to convince stressed 19-year-olds of that value by cracking down hard on something everyone does

How do I think about the ethics of enforcing the rules of an institution that they don’t take seriously, or letting things slide in the name of building a classroom that feels less like an obstacle to circumvent? Dear Troubled Teacher,    I know you said you believe in the “ineffable value of a humanities education,” but if we want to actually get clear on your dilemma, that ineffable value must be effed!  So: What is the real value of a humanities education?  Looking at the modern university, one might think the humanities aren’t so different from the STEM fields

Just as the engineering department or the math department justifies its existence by pointing to the products it creates — bridge designs, weather forecasts — humanities departments nowadays justify their existence by noting that their students create products, too: literary interpretations, cultural criticism, short films.  But let’s be real: It’s the neoliberalization of the university that has forced the humanities into that weird contortion
That’s never what they were supposed to be

Their real aim, as the philosopher Megan Fritts writes , is “the formation of human persons.”  In other words, while the purpose of other departments is ultimately to create a product, a humanities education is meant to be different, because the student herself is the product

She is what’s getting created and recreated by the learning process.  Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column? Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions
Sign up here! This vision of education — as a pursuit that’s supposed to be personally transformative — is what Aristotle proposed back in ancient Greece

He believed the real goal was not to impart knowledge, but to cultivate the virtues: honesty, justice, courage, and all the other character traits that make for a flourishing life.  But because flourishing is devalued in our hypercapitalist society, you find yourself caught between that original vision and today’s product-based, utilitarian vision

And students sense — rightly! — that generative AI proves the utilitarian vision for the humanities is a sham.  As one student said to his professor at New York University, in an effort to justify using AI to do his work for him , “You’re asking me to go from point A to point B, why wouldn’t I use a car to get there?” It’s a completely logical argument — as long as you accept the utilitarian vision.  The real solution, then, is to be honest about what the humanities are for: You’re in the business of helping students with the cultivation of their character.  I know, I know: Lots of students will say, “I don’t have time to work on cultivating my character! I just need to be able to get a job!” It’s totally fair for them to be focusing on their job prospects

But your job is to focus on something else — something that will help them flourish in the long run, even if they don’t fully see the value in it now.  Your job is to be their Aristotle.  For the ancient Greek philosopher, the mother of all virtues was phronesis , or practical wisdom
And I’d argue there’s nothing more useful you can do for your students than help them cultivate this virtue, which is made more, not less, relevant by the advent of AI
Practical wisdom goes beyond just knowing general rules — “don’t lie,” for example — and applying them mechanically like some sort of moral robot
It’s about knowing how to make good judgments when faced with the complex, dynamic situations life throws at you
Sometimes that’ll actually mean violating a classic rule (in certain cases, you should lie !)

If you’ve honed your practical wisdom, you’ll be able to discern the morally salient features of a particular situation and come up with a response that’s well-attuned to that context.  This is exactly the sort of deliberation that students will need to be good at as they step into the wider world
The breakneck pace of technological innovation means they’re going to have to choose, again and again and again, how to make use of emerging technologies — and how not to

The best training they can get now is training in how to wisely make this type of choice.  Unfortunately, that’s exactly what using generative AI in the classroom threatens to short-circuit, because it removes something incredibly valuable: friction .  AI is removing cognitive friction from education
Encountering friction is how we give our cognitive muscles a workout

Taking it out of the picture makes things easier in the short term, but in the long term, it can lead to intellectual deskilling, where our cognitive muscles gradually become weaker for lack of use.  “Practical wisdom is built up by practice just like all the other virtues, so if you don’t have the opportunity to reason and don’t have practice in deliberating about certain things, you won’t be able to deliberate well later,” philosopher of technology Shannon Vallor told me last year. “We need a lot of cognitive exercise in order to develop practical wisdom and retain it

And there is reason to worry about cognitive automation depriving us of the opportunity to build and retain those cognitive muscles.”  So, how do you help your students retain and build their phronesis? You add friction back in, by giving them as many opportunities as possible to practice deliberating and choosing.  If I were designing the curriculum, I wouldn’t do that by adopting a strict “no AI” policy
Instead, I’d be honest with students about the real benefit of the humanities and about why mindless AI cheating would be cheating themselves out of that benefit
Then, I’d offer them two choices when it comes time to write an essay: They can either write it with help from AI, or without

Both are totally fine.  But if they do get help from AI, they have to also write an in-class reflection piece, explaining why they chose to use a chatbot and how they think it changed their thinking and learning process
I’d make it shorter than the original assignment but longer than a paragraph, so it forces them to develop the very reasoning skills they were trying to avoid using
As a TA, you could suggest this to professors, but they may not go for it
Unfortunately, you’ve got limited agency here (unless you’re willing to risk your job or walk away from it)
All you can do in such a situation is exercise the agency you do have
Since you lead discussion sections, you’re well-placed to prompt your students to work their cognitive muscles in conversation
You could even stage a debate about AI: Assign half of them to argue the case for using chatbots to write papers and half of them to argue the opposite
If a professor insists on a strict “no AI” policy, and you encounter essays that seem clearly AI-written, you may have little choice but to report them
But if there’s room for doubt about a given essay, you might err on the side of leniency if the student has engaged very thoughtfully in the discussion
At least then you know they’ve achieved the most important aim

title: Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
excerpt: Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon visits Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood as she campaigns on August 29, 2026. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Last month, Flo
body: Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon visits Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood as she campaigns on August 29, 2026. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Last month, Florida state Rep
Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt

Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere
But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale

She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change.  Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state , and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel

Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise? It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money
But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch
This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing
I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country

How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida? It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for.  Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not
We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like
There’s nothing radical or extreme about that
Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election
Prominent pundits have said that Democrats should not invest in Florida, and that would amount to wasted money
Political forecasters moved the race in the Republican direction after your primary victory, arguing that the progressive politics makes it easier for Republicans to win in a state like Florida
Can you give me the case for how you can win a statewide race amongst such skepticism?  The same way that I was able to win a primary being outspent and out-raised 18 to 1
I am building a very unique, diverse coalition of people
We’ve had Republicans and independents that crossed over in the primary to vote for me in the primary
They’ve made donations.  We literally have a bunch of Republicans and libertarians who have been stating that they are voting for me because they like that I am no-nonsense
They appreciate that I am trying to put a check on what is coming out of Washington, DC, all of the cruelty and the corruption, and that is the winning message
Look, we’re up against a woman, [incumbent Republican Sen
Ashley Moody], who allowed the theft of $10 million

She allowed money to be stolen from medically needy and low-income kids, to be diverted toward two citizen-led ballot initiatives that actually caused us to not have better health in our communities.  People are frustrated, and that’s all Ashley Moody has done — just look out for herself, her campaign donors and these billionaires
People are ready for elected officials to stop bailing out these big businesses [and] actually look out for everyday people
In November 2023, you introduced a resolution to the Florida House calling for “the immediate de-escalation and ceasefire…in Israel and occupied Palestine.” It was rejected 104 to 2
And it earned you some bad blood with some of the members of the Florida Jewish Caucus
The chair actually said that the resolution was born out of ignorance and antisemitism
Obviously, the Democratic Party base has shifted on that issue over the last several years
T here’s been an open discussion about whether Joe Biden and Kamala Harris did themselves damage in the 2024 election by not breaking more explicitly with Israel’s actions in Gaza
Do you think that was a mistake for Democrats? I would say yes
I would say that we have to have really uncomfortable conversations amongst our different communities and we just have to talk
But I feel that they did do a disservice in regards to just going along with the AIPAC lobby
You had mentioned that you don’t support sending any money or any weapons to Israel at this moment, but I also wanted to ask about things like BDS, the movement to boycott, divest, or sanction Israel

I’m a Black woman who is a descendant of slaves, and who is the descendant of people from the civil rights movement, and I know how we used boycotts and we used protest to gain our civil rights for our community
You repeatedly said that you don’t support defunding the police on your website
It says that you support demilitarizing the police

And that “real safety comes from good jobs, strong schools, affordable housing, and healthcare for all — not from more cameras, more cages, and more agents.” What is the difference between that and defunding? Whatever folks think the difference is
I’m not going to box myself in because I understand how they’ll try to cut and clip things with me saying certain words
